To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of motion interchange patterns, which are local motion changes in the direction of motion, is a good way to encode motion, (2) that the use of a suppression mechanism to decouple motion edges from image edges, is beneficial for the recognition task, and (3) that the use a registration scheme that is especially fitted for our task, improves recognition performance.

(1) local changes in motion direction, (2) motion edges and (3) global camera motion are important for action recognition in unconstrained videos, and (4) a combination of all three leads to the state-of-the-art results.
motion interchange patterns, a combination of local motion changes and motion edge suppression, is an effective way of capturing motion information for action recognition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of action recognition in unconstrained videos, and our contribution is threefold.
the development of a robust motion representation for action recognition in uncontrolled videos.
the development of novel motion-based features for action recognition in videos, which are robust to viewpoint and illumination changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have shown that the use of motion interchange patterns, combined with a suppression scheme for image and motion edges, and a registration scheme that is able to handle global camera motion, is a powerful approach for action recognition in unconstrained videos, and that our method achieves state-of-the- art performance on several benchmarks.
our approach outperforms all previous state-of-the-art approaches in all the considered datasets.

the presented methods achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in the most recent challenging benchmarks, and that they can be applied in real-world scenarios where the quality of video is less than ideal and where the viewpoint is not static and often not controlled.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed motion interchange pattern (MIP) features are able to encode local motion changes and are robust to global camera motion.
we propose a novel motion encoding scheme, based on the motion interchange patterns of the local motion directions, and a new image registration scheme for global motion compensation.
our method is the first to achieve a 90% accuracy on the UCF-11 dataset and a 75% accuracy on the HMDB-51 dataset.
The main takeaway from our work is that
local changes in motion direction, which we call motion interchange patterns (MIPs), are a strong indicator of human actions.
the motion encoding can be simplified by using a single motion descriptor that is robust to viewpoint changes and can capture the motion changes of the action in the video.

motion encoding and image registration can be used as an alternative to the standard spatiotemporal encoding, and that the resulting representations can outperform the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy.
